newsitem.title: CROATIA: US envoy upbeat on return of rebel Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: US envoy upbeat on return of rebel Serb enclave.

text.p: A U.S. envoy voiced optimism on Wednesday about the return of the last rebel Serb enclave to Croatian rule and said he would soon visit Eastern Slavonia to drive home the message there was no more time for negotiations.

"The process of reintegration is, I think, going very well. It is speeding up towards July 15," ambassador Peter Galbraith told reporters after he and European Union ambassadors met Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic in the Croatian capital.
Eastern Slavonia, which seceded from Croatia in 1991, opposing Zagreb's drive for independence from federal Yugoslavia, is monitored by about 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers (UNTAES).
The UNTAES mandate ends on July 15, when Croatia wants to assume full control of the enclave. Elections for a local administration are scheduled for March 16.
The United Nations Security Council has endorsed a package of human and minority rights Zagreb offered to the Serbs and gave it a green light to go ahead with the elections.
"We made clear (to Croatia) that we expect the conditions of the (package) will be fully carried out, those conditions are preconditions for the holding of the elections," Galbraith said.
He said the diplomats won assurances from Granic that Zagreb would stick to its commitments and was considering "a package of further measures intended to reassure the local (Serb) population".

Galbraith and ambassadors from Russia, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium and Netherlands will travel to Eastern Slavonia's biggest town of Vukovar on Thursday for talks with local Serb leaders.

"We'll tell them the Croatian letter (of rights) represents a very positive step, that there is no more time for negotiation, that measures are in place to protect the rights of the Serbian population," Galbraith told reporters.
"The next step is up to them and that is to participate fully in the upcoming election and to exercise their rights through political process," he added.
The diplomat said only a small number of militant Serbs wanted to leave Croatia and were staging incidents to impede the reintegration.
A Belgian peacekeeper was killed, while a Jordanian soldier and an UNTAES civilian officer from Ivory Coast were wounded in a shooting attack in the enclave on Saturday.

The Croatian government blamed the incident on local Serb extremists reluctant to accept the region's reintegration into Croatia, while U.N. officials described it as an isolated criminal act rather than politically motivated.
"These extremists cannot be allowed to impede the process," Galbraith said.
Croatian state television reported on Wednesday the local Serb assembly in Vukovar had pledged its support to the process of reintegration and condemned the growing number of incidents.
Galbraith said he had been informed the assembly also vowed to urge the Serbs "to stay and participate in the political process".
Croatia recaptured the other two Serb enclaves in two military actions in 1995, prompting up to 200,000 Serbs to flee for safety.
